implementation_notes: A Ruby block or Proc captures its binding, and a Proc created with 'lambda' enforces arity while a bare block (Proc.new-style) does not - 'yield' and 'define_method' differ accordingly. Procs always capture 'self' from the definition site, which is why 'instance_exec' and 'define_method' exist: they run a block against a different receiver without losing the captured locals. Method objects (obj.method(:name).to_proc) are the picklable-adjacent form, but a plain Proc still cannot be marshalled across a process boundary. Ruby 3 keyword-argument separation makes it easy to get a lambda's signature subtly wrong when passing blocks across layers.
idiom_name: block or Proc capturing its binding; define_method to bind to an instance
code_sketch:
def make_counter
  n = 0
  -> { n += 1 }            # lambda enforces arity
end

class Sorter
  def initialize(rows); @rows = rows; end
  def by_deadline
    # define_method runs the block against self and keeps captured locals
    define_method(:cmp) { |a, b| a.deadline <=> b.deadline }
  end
end

[3, 1, 2].sort_by { |r| r.deadline }   # block captures nothing; keeps it simple
pitfalls: A Proc is not picklable, so it cannot cross a Marshal or a process boundary - use Method objects or a top-level method.
Blocks capture self, so instance_exec and define_method are the tools for rebinding the receiver without losing captured locals.
Proc.new versus lambda differs in arity checking and in return semantics; mixing them silently changes which 'return' you wrote.
Ruby 3 keyword arguments are separated from positional ones, so a lambda with optional keyword args called through method forwarding needs explicit **.
